sprints.notes: C programming curriculum — the foundation of systems programming. Fundamentals: compilation (gcc, clang, Makefile), data types, operators, control flow, functions, arrays, strings (null-terminated), printf/scanf. Pointers and memory: pointer arithmetic, pointer-to-pointer, function pointers, dynamic memory (malloc, calloc, realloc, free), memory leaks, dangling pointers, stack vs heap. Data structures in C: linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables (all manual). File I/O: fopen/fread/fwrite, binary files, file descriptors (open/read/write). Advanced: preprocessor directives, structs/unions/enums, bit manipulation, volatile/const qualifiers, variadic functions, inline assembly basics. Systems programming: POSIX API, process management (fork, exec, wait), signals, pipes, sockets, shared memory, semaphores, pthreads. Security relevance: buffer overflows (stack smashing, heap overflow), format string vulnerabilities, integer overflow, use-after-free — understanding these in C is essential for exploit development and secure coding. Cross-references forge house for embedded/hardware applications.

sprints.title: Code Armory — C++ (OOP, STL, and modern C++ features)
sprints.notes: C++ curriculum building on C foundations. Core OOP: classes, constructors/destructors, inheritance (single, multiple, virtual), polymorphism, operator overloading, friend functions, abstract classes. STL: containers (vector, list, deque, map, unordered_map, set, stack, queue, priority_queue), iterators, algorithms (sort, find, transform, accumulate), function objects. Modern C++ (C++11/14/17/20): auto, range-based for, smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr), move semantics, rvalue references, lambda expressions, constexpr, structured bindings, std::optional/variant/any, concepts (C++20), coroutines (C++20), ranges (C++20), modules (C++20). Memory management: RAII pattern, custom allocators, memory pools. Templates: function/class templates, template specialization, variadic templates, SFINAE, type traits. Build systems: CMake, Conan. Testing: Google Test, Catch2. Security: C++ memory safety challenges (same as C plus object-oriented pitfalls), smart pointer best practices for vulnerability prevention. Applications: game engines, performance-critical security tools, reverse engineering targets.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Go (cloud tooling and concurrent programming)
sprints.notes: Go curriculum — the language of cloud-native and security tooling. Fundamentals: packages, variables, types, functions (multiple return values), control flow, arrays/slices/maps, structs, methods, interfaces, error handling (explicit, no exceptions). Concurrency: goroutines, channels (buffered/unbuffered), select statement, sync package (Mutex, WaitGroup, Once), context package for cancellation/timeouts, common concurrency patterns (fan-in, fan-out, pipeline, worker pool). Standard library deep-dive: net/http (both client and server), encoding/json, os/exec, io, bufio, testing, flag, fmt, log, crypto. Intermediate: embedding, type assertions, reflection, generics (Go 1.18+), build tags, cross-compilation, profiling (pprof). Advanced: internal architecture (scheduler, GC), CGO, unsafe package. Ecosystem: Go modules, popular frameworks (Gin, Echo, Fiber), CLI tools (cobra, viper), gRPC, Protocol Buffers. Security applications: Go is THE language for security tools (Nuclei, subfinder, httpx, ffuf, Amass are all Go) — building custom scanners, port scanners, brute-forcers, API clients, reverse shells. Cross-references cloud house for infrastructure tooling.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Rust (memory-safe systems programming)
sprints.notes: Rust curriculum — memory safety without garbage collection. Fundamentals: cargo, variables (immutability by default), data types, functions, control flow, ownership (THE key concept), borrowing and references, lifetimes, slices. Data structures: structs, enums (with data), pattern matching, Option/Result types, error handling (? operator). Traits and generics: trait definitions, trait bounds, generic functions/structs, associated types, trait objects (dyn). Collections: Vec, HashMap, HashSet, String vs &str. Concurrency: threads, message passing (mpsc), shared state (Mutex, Arc), Send/Sync traits, fearless concurrency. Advanced: closures, iterators, smart pointers (Box, Rc, RefCell), unsafe Rust (raw pointers, FFI), macros (declarative and procedural), async/await (tokio, async-std). Ecosystem: serde (serialization), reqwest (HTTP), clap (CLI), actix-web/axum (web), sqlx (database). Security relevance: Rust eliminates entire vulnerability classes (buffer overflow, use-after-free, data races) — understanding WHY teaches secure programming principles applicable to any language. Growing adoption in security tools (ripgrep, bat, fd, rustscan).

sprints.title: Code Armory — Java (enterprise, Android, and security frameworks)
sprints.notes: Java curriculum — enterprise backbone and Android foundation. Fundamentals: JDK setup, data types, operators, control flow, OOP (classes, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, encapsulation), interfaces, abstract classes, packages, access modifiers. Intermediate: collections framework (List, Set, Map, Queue, Iterator), generics, exception handling, I/O streams, NIO, serialization, annotations, enums, inner classes, lambda expressions, Stream API, Optional. Advanced: JVM internals (class loading, memory model, garbage collection), multithreading (Thread, Runnable, ExecutorService, CompletableFuture, synchronized, volatile, concurrent collections), reflection, custom annotations, design patterns in Java. Build tools: Maven, Gradle. Testing: JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ. Frameworks: Spring Boot (REST APIs, dependency injection, security), Hibernate/JPA. Security: Java deserialization vulnerabilities (ysoserial, gadget chains), JNDI injection (Log4Shell was Java), XXE via XML parsers, secure coding with OWASP ESAPI, Java Cryptography Architecture (JCA). Android overview: Activity lifecycle, Intents, UI basics.

sprints.title: Code Armory — C# and .NET (Windows development and enterprise)
sprints.notes: C# and .NET curriculum. Fundamentals: .NET ecosystem overview (.NET 6/7/8, .NET Framework vs .NET Core), data types, variables, operators, control flow, OOP (classes, structs, interfaces, inheritance, polymorphism), properties, indexers, delegates, events, generics. Intermediate: LINQ (query and method syntax), collections, async/await (Task, Task<T>, ValueTask), exception handling patterns, nullable reference types, pattern matching, records, file I/O. Advanced: reflection, attributes, expression trees, span/memory, source generators, dependency injection, middleware pipeline. Frameworks: ASP.NET Core (MVC, Razor Pages, Blazor, Minimal APIs, SignalR), Entity Framework Core, WPF/WinUI for desktop. Testing: xUnit, NUnit, Moq, FluentAssertions. Security: .NET security model, Data Protection API, Identity framework, anti-forgery tokens, CORS configuration, .NET deserialization vulnerabilities, PowerShell integration for security tooling. Cross-platform with .NET MAUI. Relevant for enterprise security assessment and Windows-heavy environments.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Bash and shell scripting (system administration and automation)
sprints.notes: Bash and shell scripting curriculum — the universal glue language. Fundamentals: shell basics (sh vs bash vs zsh), variables, quoting (single vs double vs backtick), command substitution, arithmetic, test conditions ([ ] vs [[ ]]), if/elif/else, case statements, for/while/until loops, functions. Text processing: pipes and redirection (stdin/stdout/stderr, >, >>, 2>&1, |, tee), grep/egrep, sed (substitution, deletion, insertion), awk (field processing, patterns, actions), cut, sort, uniq, tr, wc, head/tail, xargs. Intermediate: arrays (indexed and associative), string manipulation (substring, replacement), parameter expansion, here documents, process substitution, trap (signal handling), exit codes, debugging (set -x, set -e, set -o pipefail). Advanced: coproc, file descriptor manipulation, /proc and /sys filesystem interaction, cron/systemd timers, expect scripting, bash completion. Security applications: log parsing, automated scanning scripts, evidence collection, incident response automation, SIEM data extraction, system hardening verification scripts, compliance checking. Cross-references script house and linux house.

sprints.title: Code Armory — PowerShell (Windows administration and security)
sprints.notes: PowerShell curriculum — Windows automation and security powerhouse. Fundamentals: cmdlets (Verb-Noun convention), pipeline, objects (everything is an object), variables, data types, operators, comparison operators, control flow, functions (params, begin/process/end), modules, help system (Get-Help, Get-Command, Get-Member). Intermediate: regular expressions, file/folder operations, registry access, WMI/CIM queries, remoting (Enter-PSSession, Invoke-Command), PSCredential/SecureString, error handling (try/catch/finally, $ErrorActionPreference), output formatting (Format-Table, Format-List, ConvertTo-Json/CSV/HTML). Advanced: custom classes, DSC (Desired State Configuration), PowerShell providers, runspaces for parallelism, script signing, constrained language mode, JEA (Just Enough Administration). Security applications: Active Directory enumeration and management, event log analysis, incident response data collection, malware analysis (file hashing, string extraction, process inspection), AMSI bypass understanding (defensive), PowerShell-based attack tools analysis (PowerSploit, Empire — for blue team understanding), hardening and audit scripts, compliance verification. Cross-references WSA (Windows Server Admin) modules.

sprints.title: Code Armory — SQL (database querying, management, and injection)
sprints.notes: SQL curriculum — data is everything. Fundamentals: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, data types, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT). Intermediate: JOINs (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS, self-join), GROUP BY, HAVING, aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX), subqueries (scalar, column, table, correlated), UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT, CASE expressions, views, indexes (B-tree, hash, composite), EXPLAIN/ANALYZE. Advanced: window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LEAD, LAG, SUM OVER), CTEs (WITH clause, recursive CTEs), transactions (ACID, isolation levels), stored procedures, triggers, user-defined functions, database administration (backups, replication, partitioning). Database engines: MySQL/MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQLite, SQL Server — syntax differences and strengths. NoSQL overview: MongoDB queries, Redis commands, Elasticsearch. Security: SQL injection deep-dive (this IS the language being injected — understanding SQL is understanding SQLi), parameterized queries, stored procedure injection, blind SQL injection techniques, second-order injection, NoSQL injection (MongoDB $gt/$ne operators), database hardening (least privilege, audit logging).

sprints.title: Code Armory — PHP (web development and legacy codebase security)
sprints.notes: PHP curriculum — still powers 77% of the web. Fundamentals: variables, types, operators, strings (single/double-quoted, heredoc), arrays (indexed, associative, multidimensional), control structures, functions, superglobals ($_GET, $_POST, $_SESSION, $_COOKIE, $_SERVER, $_FILES). OOP: classes, interfaces, traits, abstract classes, namespaces, autoloading (PSR-4), type declarations, union types (PHP 8), enums (PHP 8.1). Web development: form handling, file uploads, sessions and cookies, database access (PDO, prepared statements), templating. Modern PHP: Composer (dependency management), PSR standards, PHP 8.x features (named arguments, match expression, fibers, readonly properties, constructor promotion). Frameworks: Laravel (routing, Eloquent ORM, Blade templates, middleware, Artisan CLI), Symfony (components, Doctrine). Security: PHP is a goldmine for bug hunters — type juggling (== vs ===), deserialization (unserialize), file inclusion (LFI/RFI), command injection (shell_exec, system, exec, backticks), SSRF via file_get_contents, preg_replace /e flag (deprecated but legacy), register_globals legacy issues, PHP filter chains. Understanding PHP security is critical because so many bug bounty targets run PHP.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Ruby (scripting, web development, and security tools)
sprints.notes: Ruby curriculum — elegant scripting and Metasploit's backbone. Fundamentals: variables, data types, operators, strings (interpolation, methods), arrays, hashes, symbols, control flow, iterators (each, map, select, reduce), blocks/procs/lambdas, methods, classes, modules (mixins). Intermediate: file I/O, regular expressions, exception handling, gems (bundler), testing (RSpec, Minitest), metaprogramming (method_missing, define_method, send, eval), open classes (monkey patching). Ruby on Rails: MVC architecture, ActiveRecord (migrations, associations, validations, queries), routing, controllers, views (ERB), ActionCable (WebSockets), ActiveJob, API mode. Security relevance: Metasploit Framework is written in Ruby — understanding Ruby is essential for writing/modifying Metasploit modules, custom exploits, and auxiliary scripts. Rails security: mass assignment, CSRF protection, SQL injection via ActiveRecord, remote code execution via deserialization (Marshal.load), ERB/SSTI, Brakeman (SAST for Rails). Also used in: Vagrant, Chef, WPScan (WordPress scanner).

sprints.title: Code Armory — Assembly language (x86/x64, reverse engineering foundations)
sprints.notes: Assembly language curriculum — understanding the machine. x86/x64 fundamentals: registers (general purpose, segment, flags, instruction pointer), memory addressing modes, data movement (MOV, LEA, PUSH, POP), arithmetic (ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, INC, DEC), logic (AND, OR, XOR, NOT, SHL, SHR), comparison/branching (CMP, TEST, JMP, JE, JNE, JG, JL), function calls (CALL, RET, stack frames, calling conventions — cdecl, stdcall, fastcall, System V AMD64 ABI). Memory: stack operations, heap concepts, memory layout (text, data, BSS, heap, stack), endianness. System calls: Linux syscalls (int 0x80, syscall instruction), Windows API calls. Tools: NASM, GAS (AT&T vs Intel syntax), GDB/radare2/IDA for debugging/disassembly, objdump, strace/ltrace. ARM overview: ARM vs x86, common ARM instructions, ARM in IoT/mobile. Security applications: understanding compiled code for reverse engineering, shellcode development, ROP chain construction, understanding exploit mitigations (DEP, ASLR, stack canaries, PIE) at the assembly level, malware analysis. This is the bridge between code and dark-arts for exploit development.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Swift and Kotlin (modern mobile development)
sprints.notes: Combined Swift and Kotlin curriculum — modern mobile-first languages. Swift: variables (let/var), types, optionals (?, !, guard let, if let), collections, control flow, functions, closures, OOP (classes, structs, enums, protocols, extensions), error handling (do-try-catch), generics, property wrappers, async/await (Swift 5.5), SwiftUI basics, UIKit overview. Kotlin: val/var, null safety (?., ?:, !!), data classes, sealed classes, object declarations, companion objects, extension functions, higher-order functions, coroutines (launch, async, suspend, Flow), scope functions (let, run, apply, also, with), Kotlin for Android (Activity, Fragment, ViewModel, LiveData, Room). Security perspective: mobile app security testing context — understanding how these languages compile and run helps with reverse engineering iOS/Android apps, identifying hardcoded secrets, understanding app permissions, certificate pinning implementation, biometric authentication patterns.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Lua, Perl, and R (specialized scripting languages)
sprints.notes: Three specialized scripting languages in one module. Lua: lightweight embeddable scripting — variables, tables (Lua's universal data structure), metatables, coroutines, string patterns, C API for embedding. Used in: Nmap NSE scripts (critical for security scanning), game modding (Roblox, WoW), Redis scripting, nginx/OpenResty, Wireshark dissectors. Perl: text processing powerhouse — regular expressions (Perl's crown jewel), file handling, references, hashes, modules (CPAN), one-liners for log parsing. Used in: legacy security tools, sysadmin scripts, Nikto (web scanner), text processing pipelines. R: statistical computing and data analysis — vectors, data frames, packages (tidyverse, ggplot2, dplyr), statistical functions, data visualization, reading CSV/JSON. Used in: security analytics, threat intelligence data analysis, log analysis visualization, SOC metrics dashboards, machine learning for anomaly detection. Each language gets: fundamentals, practical exercises, and security-specific applications.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Language comparison tool and syntax reference
sprints.notes: Interactive language comparison and quick-reference applet. Build a side-by-side code comparison tool where students can select 2-4 languages and see equivalent code for common operations: Hello World, variable declaration, conditionals, loops, functions, classes/structs, error handling, file reading, HTTP request, JSON parsing, list/array operations, string manipulation, regex matching, command execution. Additional features: syntax cheat sheets (one-page printable reference per language), paradigm comparison chart (which languages support which paradigms), performance benchmarks for common operations, memory model comparison (GC vs manual vs ownership), ecosystem comparison (package manager, testing framework, build tools, IDE support). Rosetta Stone mode: paste code in one language, see equivalent in another (reference only, not a transpiler). Built as an interactive applet using Prime's existing applet infrastructure. Useful for polyglot developers and for students transitioning between languages.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Per-language coding challenges and exercises
sprints.notes: Hands-on coding challenges for each language. Difficulty tiers: Apprentice (10 challenges per language — basics, string manipulation, math), Journeyman (10 per language — data structures, algorithms, file I/O), Master (5 per language — complex projects, real-world scenarios). Challenge types: algorithm challenges (sorting, searching, graph traversal in target language), security challenges (write a port scanner in Go, build an XSS filter in Python, implement AES encryption in C), project challenges (build a CLI tool, create a REST API, write a web scraper). Auto-graded where possible using Prime's challenge infrastructure. Leaderboard integration per language. Track which languages a student has completed challenges in — award 'Polyglot' badge at 5 languages, 'Omniglot' at 10. Include: community-submitted challenges with review pipeline, weekly challenge rotations.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Security-focused language selection guide
sprints.notes: Guide mapping cybersecurity career paths to recommended programming languages. Career path recommendations: SOC Analyst (Python, Bash, PowerShell, SQL), Penetration Tester (Python, Bash, Go, Ruby, Assembly), Malware Analyst (C, C++, Assembly, Python), Web App Security (JavaScript, PHP, Python, SQL), Cloud Security Engineer (Python, Go, Bash, Terraform/HCL), DevSecOps (Python, Bash, Go, YAML/HCL), Threat Intelligence (Python, R, SQL), Incident Responder (Python, Bash, PowerShell), Firmware/IoT Security (C, C++, Assembly, Python), GRC/Compliance (SQL, Python, PowerShell). For each career: why these languages matter, in what order to learn them, minimum proficiency needed, and which PL modules to complete. Include industry survey data on most-requested languages in security job postings. Interactive quiz: 'What should I learn next?' based on current skills and career goals. Cross-references all houses that use programming.

sprints.title: The Backbone — Design advanced networking hub page and curriculum map
sprints.notes: Design 'The Backbone' — the advanced networking curriculum hub within House of the Web. This sits above the existing Network+ content as the next tier for students who have completed foundational networking. Hub page features: curriculum map showing all advanced tracks (Data Center, Service Provider, High-Performance, Programmability, Wireless, WAN, Security), prerequisite checker (verifies Network+ or CCNA-level completion), difficulty indicators (Advanced / Expert / Specialist), career path mapping (Network Architect, DC Network Engineer, SP Engineer, Wireless Architect). Navigation: accessible from web house as 'Advanced Studies' section. Each track gets its own card with description, module count, estimated hours, and industry certifications it aligns with. Register all AN content in content-registry.js with 'advanced-networking' topic tag.

sprints.title: The Backbone — BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) deep-dive
sprints.notes: Comprehensive BGP curriculum — the protocol that runs the internet. Fundamentals: autonomous systems (ASN), iBGP vs eBGP, BGP neighbor relationships (states: Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, Established), BGP message types (Open, Update, Keepalive, Notification), path attributes (AS-Path, Next-Hop, Local Preference, MED, Origin, Weight, Community). Route selection: BGP best path algorithm (13-step decision process), route manipulation with route-maps, prefix lists, AS-path access lists, communities (standard, extended, large), route filtering and policy control. Advanced: BGP confederations, route reflectors, BGP graceful restart, Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD), BGP Flowspec (DDoS mitigation), BGP security (RPKI, ROA, BGPsec, prefix hijack detection), BGP in data center (eBGP as underlay in Clos/Spine-Leaf), BGP EVPN for VXLAN overlay. Labs: multi-AS topology simulation, route leak scenarios, prefix hijack detection exercise, route policy design. Interactive applets: BGP path selection visualizer, AS topology mapper. Security angle: BGP hijacking attacks, route leak incidents (Pakistan/YouTube, Rostelecom), RPKI deployment for defense.

sprints.title: The Backbone — MPLS and service provider technologies
sprints.notes: MPLS and SP networking curriculum. MPLS fundamentals: label switching concepts, Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), MPLS forwarding (push, swap, pop, PHP — penultimate hop popping), Label Switched Paths (LSPs), MPLS label stack. MPLS VPN: L3VPN (VRF, RD, RT, MP-BGP for VPNv4/v6 address families, PE-CE routing), L2VPN (VPLS, VPWS, pseudowires), EVPN (next-gen L2/L3 VPN). Traffic Engineering: RSVP-TE, constrained SPF, explicit paths, bandwidth reservation, fast reroute (FRR — facility backup, one-to-one backup). Segment Routing: SR-MPLS (replacing LDP and RSVP-TE), node/adjacency SIDs, Topology Independent LBF (TI-LFA), SR-TE policies. SP architecture: core/aggregation/access design, peering and transit, IXP (Internet Exchange Point) design, carrier Ethernet (MEF standards — E-Line, E-LAN, E-Tree). Labs: L3VPN configuration, traffic engineering path setup, SR migration scenario. Security: MPLS inherent isolation properties, VPN security considerations, label spoofing risks.

sprints.title: The Backbone — Data center networking and fabric architecture
sprints.notes: Data center network architecture curriculum. DC topology evolution: traditional 3-tier (core/aggregation/access) → 2-tier Spine-Leaf (Clos network), fat-tree architecture, why Spine-Leaf won (east-west traffic patterns, equal-cost paths, predictable latency). Overlay networking: VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN — 16M segment IDs vs 4K VLANs, MAC-in-UDP encapsulation, VTEP, BUM traffic handling), NVGRE, Geneve, EVPN-VXLAN (control plane for VXLAN — BGP EVPN with type-2/type-5 routes, distributed anycast gateway, ARP suppression). Underlay design: eBGP as underlay protocol (unnumbered interfaces, ASN allocation), OSPF vs IS-IS vs BGP for DC underlay, ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path), IP fabric. DC interconnect: DCI technologies, OTV (Overlay Transport Virtualization), stretched VLANs (why to avoid), EVPN multi-site. Physical layer: 25G/100G/400G/800G Ethernet, DAC vs AOC vs fiber optics, breakout cables. Vendors: Cisco ACI (Application Centric Infrastructure), Arista CloudVision, Juniper QFX/Apstra, SONiC (open source NOS). Labs: Spine-Leaf design exercise, VXLAN-EVPN configuration, DC capacity planning.

sprints.title: The Backbone — InfiniBand, RDMA, and high-performance networking
sprints.notes: High-performance networking curriculum — where microseconds matter. InfiniBand architecture: IB fundamentals (channel adapters — HCA/TCA, switches, routers, subnet manager), IB layers (physical, link, network, transport), data rates (SDR 10G → HDR 200G → NDR 400G → XDR 800G), IB addressing (GID, LID, GUID), partitions (P_Keys), virtual lanes. RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access): zero-copy networking, kernel bypass, RDMA verbs API (ibv_post_send, ibv_post_recv, ibv_poll_cq), memory registration, queue pairs (QP), completion queues (CQ), protection domains. RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE): RoCEv1 (L2 only) vs RoCEv2 (routable, UDP encapsulation), Priority Flow Control (PFC), ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification), lossless Ethernet requirements, DCQCN congestion control. iWARP: RDMA over TCP, comparison with RoCE. Applications: HPC clusters (MPI over RDMA), AI/ML training (GPU-to-GPU communication — NCCL, GPUDirect RDMA), storage networking (NVMe-oF — NVMe over Fabrics), financial trading (ultra-low-latency market data), database clustering. Tools: perftest (ib_read_bw, ib_write_lat), ibstat, ibdiagnet, rdma-core, OFED drivers. Labs: RDMA performance benchmarking, RoCEv2 lossless Ethernet configuration, InfiniBand subnet manager setup. Security: IB partition security model, RDMA attack surface (memory exposure risks), securing RDMA-enabled storage networks.

sprints.title: The Backbone — Software-Defined Networking and network programmability
sprints.notes: SDN and network programmability curriculum — beyond the intro slides. SDN architecture: control plane / data plane / management plane separation, SDN controllers (OpenDaylight, ONOS, Ryu, Floodlight), southbound interfaces (OpenFlow protocol — match/action tables, flow entries, group tables, meters), northbound APIs (REST). Network automation: NETCONF (XML-based, SSH transport, get/edit-config/commit), RESTCONF (HTTP-based, JSON/XML), YANG data models (RFC 7950 — containers, lists, leaves, augmentations, deviations), gNMI/gNOI (gRPC-based, streaming telemetry). Automation tools: Ansible for networking (ios_config, eos_config, nxos_config modules, Jinja2 templates, inventory management), Nornir (Python framework), NAPALM (multi-vendor abstraction), Netmiko (SSH library for network devices), Batfish (config analysis and validation). Infrastructure as Code: Terraform for networking (provider plugins for Cisco, Arista, Palo Alto), GitOps for network configs. Streaming telemetry: model-driven telemetry vs SNMP polling, dial-in vs dial-out, gRPC/gNMI collectors, TIG stack (Telegraf/InfluxDB/Grafana) for visualization. Labs: OpenFlow flow table programming, Ansible playbook for multi-switch VLAN provisioning, Python script for config backup with Netmiko, YANG model exploration with pyang. Cross-references code house (Python) and script house (automation).

sprints.title: The Backbone — Advanced SD-WAN and WAN optimization
sprints.notes: SD-WAN deep-dive beyond the existing introductory slides. SD-WAN architecture: overlay/underlay separation, control plane (vManage, vSmart controllers), data plane (vEdge/cEdge), OMP (Overlay Management Protocol), TLOC (Transport Locator). Advanced policies: application-aware routing (DPI, SLA metrics — latency, jitter, loss), centralized vs localized policies, traffic engineering policies, security policies (embedded firewall, IPS, URL filtering, AMP, DNS-layer security). Multi-cloud integration: SD-WAN to cloud on-ramps (AWS Transit Gateway, Azure Virtual WAN, GCP Partner Interconnect), SaaS optimization (Office 365, Salesforce direct cloud access), cloud-hosted controllers. WAN optimization: TCP optimization (window scaling, selective ACK), data deduplication, compression, application acceleration, forward error correction. Competing architectures: Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela), Fortinet SD-WAN, VMware SD-WAN (VeloCloud), Palo Alto Prisma SD-WAN, Versa Networks, SASE convergence (SD-WAN + SSE). Design: hub-and-spoke vs full-mesh vs hybrid, bandwidth aggregation, transport independence (MPLS + broadband + LTE/5G), migration from traditional WAN. Security: SD-WAN security integration, SASE (Secure Access Service Edge), zero-trust WAN.

sprints.title: The Backbone — Advanced wireless (Wi-Fi 6/6E/7, enterprise, mesh)
sprints.notes: Advanced wireless networking beyond 802.11 basics. Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax): OFDMA (uplink and downlink), MU-MIMO (8x8), BSS Coloring (spatial reuse), TWT (Target Wake Time), 1024-QAM. Wi-Fi 6E: 6 GHz band (UNII-5 through UNII-8), 160 MHz channels, AFC (Automated Frequency Coordination), reduced interference (greenfield band). Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be): 320 MHz channels, 4096-QAM, Multi-Link Operation (MLO), preamble puncturing, 36 Gbps theoretical max. Enterprise wireless: controller-based vs controllerless architectures, Cisco Catalyst Wireless (WLC 9800), Aruba Central, Meraki cloud-managed, Mist AI-driven. Design: site surveys (predictive vs passive vs active), AP placement, channel planning (2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz vs 6 GHz), power levels, high-density deployments (stadiums, auditoriums), roaming (802.11r/k/v, OKC). Mesh networking: mesh vs traditional, mesh protocols (802.11s), backhaul design, mesh in outdoor/campus deployments. Wireless security: WPA3 (SAE, 192-bit mode, OWE for open networks), EAP methods (PEAP, EAP-TLS, EAP-TTLS), RADIUS/802.1X, wireless IDS/IPS (rogue AP detection, deauth attack detection), WIPS, RF jamming awareness. Labs: wireless site survey exercise, enterprise WLAN design, wireless security audit.

sprints.title: The Backbone — Optical networking and physical layer technologies
sprints.notes: Optical and physical layer networking — the foundation everything rides on. Fiber optics deep-dive: single-mode vs multi-mode (OS1/OS2, OM1-OM5), connectors (LC, SC, MTP/MPO, FC), splicing (fusion vs mechanical), OTDR testing and fiber characterization, bend radius and loss budget calculations. DWDM (Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing): wavelength grid (ITU-T G.694.1), DWDM components (transponders, multiplexers, amplifiers — EDFA, Raman), ROADM (Reconfigurable Optical Add-Drop Multiplexer), coherent optics (DP-QPSK, 16QAM, probabilistic constellation shaping), 100G/400G/800G ZR/ZR+ pluggable optics. SONET/SDH: legacy but still relevant — STS levels, virtual tributaries, APS (Automatic Protection Switching), ring architectures (BLSR, UPSR). Submarine cables: transoceanic cable systems, repeaters, branching units, cable landing stations, wet plant vs dry plant. Data center optics: transceiver types (SFP, SFP+, SFP28, QSFP28, QSFP-DD, OSFP), reach classifications (SR, LR, ER, ZR), silicon photonics, co-packaged optics (CPO) for next-gen switches. Free-space optics and emerging: FSO for last-mile, Li-Fi concepts, hollow-core fiber. Security: fiber tapping (bend-radius tapping, splitter insertion), physical layer security monitoring, quantum key distribution (QKD) over fiber.

sprints.title: The Backbone — Advanced IPv6 and internet protocol evolution
sprints.notes: Advanced IPv6 beyond the basics already covered. Transition mechanisms: dual-stack deployment strategies, tunneling (6to4, ISATAP, 6in4, 6rd — Rapid Deployment), translation (NAT64/DNS64, SIIT, 464XLAT, MAP-T/MAP-E). Advanced addressing: ULA (Unique Local Address), anycast, SLAAC vs DHCPv6 (stateless vs stateful), privacy extensions (RFC 4941), temporary addresses, stable SLAAC (RFC 7217). Routing: OSPFv3 (multi-AF support), MP-BGP for IPv6 (AFI/SAFI), IS-IS for IPv6, IPv6 routing security (RA Guard, DHCPv6 Shield, ND Inspection). Advanced features: IPv6 extension headers (hop-by-hop, routing, fragment, destination, AH, ESP), flow labels, jumbograms, SRv6 (Segment Routing over IPv6 — next-gen traffic engineering, network programming via SRH). IPv6 security: NDP attacks (RA spoofing, NDP cache poisoning), extension header abuse (evasion, fragmentation attacks), IPv6 scanning challenges (address space too large for brute-force), IPv6 firewall considerations (implicit tunnels, privacy addresses), RFC 7707 (Network Reconnaissance in IPv6). Deployment case studies: major ISP IPv6 rollouts, enterprise dual-stack migrations, IPv6-only networks (T-Mobile, Apple requirements). Labs: dual-stack migration planning, NAT64 configuration, IPv6 ACL design, NDP security implementation.

sprints.title: The Backbone — Network security architecture and zero trust
sprints.notes: Advanced network security architecture beyond basic firewalls. Next-gen firewalls: application-layer inspection (Palo Alto, Fortinet, Check Point), policy design (zone-based vs interface-based), SSL/TLS inspection (decrypt/re-encrypt, certificate pinning challenges), threat intelligence feeds integration. Microsegmentation: host-based segmentation (VMware NSX, Cisco ACI contracts, Illumio), identity-based policies, east-west traffic inspection, workload-level firewalls. Zero Trust Network Architecture: NIST SP 800-207, BeyondCorp model, SDP (Software-Defined Perimeter), ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) vs VPN, continuous verification, policy engine / policy administrator / policy enforcement point. Network Access Control: 802.1X deployment (wired and wireless), MAB (MAC Authentication Bypass), profiling, posture assessment, guest networking, BYOD policies, ISE/ClearPass/PacketFence. Advanced IDS/IPS: Suricata/Snort rule writing, signature vs behavioral detection, network-based vs host-based, evasion techniques (fragmentation, encoding, tunneling), encrypted traffic analysis (JA3/JA4 fingerprinting, ETA). DDoS mitigation: volumetric/protocol/application-layer attacks, scrubbing centers, BGP Flowspec, Anycast-based mitigation, cloud-based DDoS protection (Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS Shield). Cross-references shield house for defensive perspective.

sprints.title: The Backbone — Network forensics and deep packet analysis
sprints.notes: Network forensics and traffic analysis curriculum. Packet capture: tcpdump (advanced filters, BPF syntax), Wireshark (display filters, conversation tracking, stream reassembly, protocol dissectors, custom columns, coloring rules, profiles), tshark for scripting, packet brokers and TAPs vs SPAN ports, full packet capture at scale (Arkime/Moloch, Zeek/Bro). Protocol analysis: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC) analysis, TLS handshake analysis (ClientHello, certificates, cipher suites), DNS analysis (query patterns, tunneling detection, DGA detection), SMB/CIFS analysis, Kerberos analysis. Forensic techniques: timeline reconstruction from pcaps, lateral movement detection, data exfiltration identification (DNS tunneling, ICMP tunneling, steganography in traffic), C2 beacon detection (jitter analysis, callback patterns), encrypted traffic analysis without decryption (metadata, flow analysis, JA3/JA4 hashing). Zeek/Bro: scripting language, log formats (conn.log, dns.log, http.log, ssl.log, files.log), custom scripts for threat detection, Zeek packages. NetFlow/IPFIX: flow collection and analysis, flow-based anomaly detection, SiLK tools, nfdump/nfsen, ElastiFlow. Labs: PCAP analysis challenges (CTF-style), lateral movement detection in captures, C2 traffic identification, DNS tunneling detection exercise. Cross-references eye house (monitoring) and dark-arts (offensive traffic patterns).

sprints.title: The Backbone — Advanced QoS and traffic engineering
sprints.notes: Advanced QoS beyond the existing visualizer. QoS fundamentals review: classification and marking (DSCP, CoS/802.1p, IP Precedence), trust boundaries. Queuing mechanisms: FIFO, Priority Queuing, Custom Queuing, Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ), Class-Based WFQ (CBWFQ), Low Latency Queuing (LLQ — priority + CBWFQ), Weighted Random Early Detection (WRED). Traffic policing and shaping: single-rate vs dual-rate policers (srTCM, trTCM — RFC 2697/2698), token bucket mechanics, shaping with Tc/Bc/Be, hierarchical QoS (HQoS — parent/child policies). QoS design models: DiffServ (Per-Hop Behavior — EF, AF, BE), IntServ (RSVP-based reservation — mostly historical), Cisco 4/8/12-class models, RFC 4594 (DiffServ service class recommendations). Application-specific QoS: voice (G.711, G.729 — bandwidth, jitter, delay requirements), video (adaptive bitrate, burst handling), real-time collaboration (WebRTC, Teams/Zoom), IoT traffic prioritization. Data center QoS: Priority Flow Control (PFC — IEEE 802.1Qbb), Enhanced Transmission Selection (ETS — 802.1Qaz), Data Center Bridging Exchange (DCBX), lossless Ethernet for RoCE/FCoE. Labs: multi-class QoS policy design, voice/video QoS testing with traffic generators, WRED tuning exercise.

sprints.title: The Backbone — IS-IS, EIGRP advanced, and routing protocol mastery
sprints.notes: Advanced routing protocol deep-dives. IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System): CLNS addressing (NET, NSAP), IS-IS levels (L1, L2, L1/L2), adjacency formation, TLV-based LSPs, SPF calculation, IS-IS for IP (Integrated IS-IS), IS-IS vs OSPF comparison (why ISPs prefer IS-IS), IS-IS extensions (TE, SR), multi-topology IS-IS. EIGRP advanced: DUAL algorithm deep-dive (feasibility condition, reported/feasible distance, successor/feasible successor), stub routing, route summarization, named EIGRP, EIGRP over DMVPN/LISP, EIGRP for IPv6, unequal-cost load balancing (variance), EIGRP security (authentication, route filtering). OSPF advanced: OSPF area types deep review (stub, NSSA, totally stub/NSSA), LSA types (1-7 detailed), virtual links, OSPF sham links (MPLS L3VPN), OSPFv3 (dual-stack, AF support), OSPF Graceful Restart, OSPF LSDB optimization, OSPF security (authentication, max-metric). Multi-protocol routing: VRF-lite (multi-tenant routing without MPLS), route redistribution (seed metrics, route tags, preventing loops), PBR (Policy-Based Routing). Labs: IS-IS multi-level topology, EIGRP stub hub-and-spoke, OSPF multi-area with redistribution, VRF-lite deployment.

sprints.title: The Backbone — 5G, cellular, and carrier networking
sprints.notes: Cellular and carrier networking — where wireless meets core infrastructure. 5G architecture: 5G NR (New Radio), frequency bands (sub-6 GHz, mmWave), massive MIMO, beamforming, 5G core (5GC — AMF, SMF, UPF, AUSF, UDM), network slicing (eMBB, URLLC, mMTC slices), Mobile Edge Computing (MEC), Non-Standalone (NSA) vs Standalone (SA) 5G. LTE fundamentals: EPC architecture (eNodeB, MME, SGW, PGW, HSS), bearers, handover types, VoLTE. Private 5G/LTE: CBRS (Citizens Broadband Radio Service), OnGo, private cellular for enterprise/industrial, spectrum allocation (licensed, unlicensed, shared). Backhaul and fronthaul: xHaul architectures, eCPRI, fiber backhaul, microwave backhaul, free-space optical links, small cell deployment. Carrier technologies: GPON/XGS-PON (fiber to the home), DOCSIS 3.1/4.0 (cable), DSL/G.fast (copper), fixed wireless access (FWA). Security: SIM cloning, IMSI catchers (Stingray), SS7/Diameter vulnerabilities, GTP protocol security, fake base stations, 5G security improvements (SUPI/SUCI, 256-bit keys), private 5G security considerations.

sprints.title: The Backbone — Network design and architecture capstone
sprints.notes: Capstone course pulling together all advanced networking knowledge. Design methodology: Cisco PPDIOO (Prepare, Plan, Design, Implement, Operate, Optimize), requirements gathering, business constraint analysis, scalability planning, redundancy and resilience (N+1, 2N, 2N+1). Enterprise design project: design a multi-site enterprise network from scratch — campus LAN (access/distribution/core), WAN connectivity (MPLS + SD-WAN), data center fabric (Spine-Leaf + VXLAN-EVPN), remote access (ZTNA), wireless (Wi-Fi 6E enterprise), security architecture (NGFW, microsegmentation, NAC), monitoring and management. Service provider design project: design an ISP network — BGP peering strategy, MPLS core, customer VPN services, traffic engineering, DDoS protection, IPv6 deployment. HPC/AI cluster design project: design a GPU cluster network — InfiniBand fabric, RDMA storage network, Ethernet management plane, fat-tree topology, congestion management. Deliverables for each project: topology diagram, bill of materials, IP addressing plan, routing protocol design, security policy, capacity analysis, migration plan. Peer review and instructor evaluation. This is the 'final exam' of The Backbone — demonstrates mastery across all AN modules.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Design course hub and learning path
sprints.notes: Design 'The Algorithm Chamber' — a discrete math, algorithms, and data structures course within House of Code. Hub page features: course map showing progression from foundations (discrete math) through data structures to algorithm design to advanced topics, inspired by 'Algorithms to Live By' (Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths) as a pacing and framing guide. Each chapter of the book maps to a module: real-world problems first, then the CS theory behind the solution. Structure: 4 tracks — (1) Discrete Math Foundations, (2) Data Structures, (3) Algorithm Design & Analysis, (4) Applied Algorithms & Real-World Problem Solving. Difficulty tiers: Foundation → Intermediate → Advanced → Competition/Research. Prerequisites: basic programming in any language (cross-reference PL series). Include: interactive visualizations for every algorithm, Big O complexity reference chart, 'Algorithm of the Week' spotlight. Register in content-registry.js under code house with 'algorithms', 'discrete-math', 'data-structures' topics.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Discrete mathematics foundations
sprints.notes: Discrete math foundations for CS and algorithm analysis. Logic: propositional logic (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, implication, biconditional), truth tables, logical equivalences, predicate logic (quantifiers — forall, exists), proof techniques (direct, contradiction, contrapositive, induction). Set theory: sets, subsets, power sets, Cartesian products, set operations (union, intersection, complement, difference), Venn diagrams, cardinality, countable vs uncountable sets. Relations and functions: binary relations, equivalence relations, partial orders, total orders, functions (injective, surjective, bijective), inverse functions, composition. Combinatorics: counting principles (multiplication, addition, inclusion-exclusion), permutations, combinations, binomial theorem, Pascal's triangle, pigeonhole principle, Stars and Bars. Probability: sample spaces, events, conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, expected value, variance, random variables, distributions (uniform, binomial, geometric, Poisson). Number theory: divisibility, GCD/LCM (Euclidean algorithm), modular arithmetic, prime numbers, Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, RSA connection. Each topic includes: interactive visualizations, practice problems, and real-world application examples from 'Algorithms to Live By' (e.g., Bayes' theorem for decision-making under uncertainty).

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Graph theory and network mathematics
sprints.notes: Graph theory — the mathematical backbone of networks and relationships. Fundamentals: vertices, edges, directed vs undirected, weighted vs unweighted, adjacency matrix vs adjacency list, degree (in-degree, out-degree), paths, cycles, connectivity. Graph types: complete graphs, bipartite graphs, trees, forests, DAGs (directed acyclic graphs), planar graphs, Euler's formula. Graph traversal: BFS (breadth-first search), DFS (depth-first search), topological sort, connected components, strongly connected components (Tarjan's, Kosaraju's). Shortest path: Dijkstra's algorithm, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, A* search. Minimum spanning tree: Kruskal's, Prim's. Network flow: Ford-Fulkerson, max-flow min-cut theorem, bipartite matching. Classic problems: Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP — exact, approximation, heuristics), graph coloring (chromatic number, scheduling applications), Eulerian/Hamiltonian paths, clique detection, vertex cover. Real-world applications: social network analysis, internet routing (BGP as graph problem), circuit design, dependency resolution (package managers), map coloring, airline route optimization. Interactive visualizations: animated graph algorithms, step-by-step traversal, TSP brute-force vs heuristic comparison. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: networking/social chapter.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Big O notation and complexity analysis
sprints.notes: Algorithm complexity analysis — measuring what matters. Asymptotic notation: Big O (upper bound), Big Omega (lower bound), Big Theta (tight bound), little-o, little-omega. Common complexity classes: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n) linearithmic, O(n^2) quadratic, O(n^3) cubic, O(2^n) exponential, O(n!) factorial. Analysis techniques: counting operations, identifying dominant terms, dropping constants and lower-order terms, best/worst/average case analysis, amortized analysis (aggregate, accounting, potential method). Recurrence relations: solving recurrences (substitution, recursion tree, Master theorem — T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)), common recurrence patterns (binary search, merge sort, Strassen's). Space complexity: auxiliary space vs total space, space-time tradeoffs, in-place algorithms. P vs NP: P (polynomial time), NP (nondeterministic polynomial), NP-complete (Cook-Levin theorem, SAT), NP-hard, polynomial-time reductions, why P vs NP matters for cryptography and security. Interactive tools: Big O visualizer (plot and compare growth rates), complexity quiz (guess the Big O from code snippets), recurrence solver. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: computational kindness — when it's OK to use a 'worse' algorithm because the constant factors matter more than asymptotic behavior.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Data structures deep-dive
sprints.notes: Core data structures with complexity analysis and implementation. Linear structures: arrays (static vs dynamic, amortized doubling), linked lists (singly, doubly, circular), stacks (LIFO — applications: expression evaluation, backtracking, undo), queues (FIFO, circular queue, deque, priority queue). Trees: binary trees, binary search trees (BST — insert, delete, search, traversals: inorder, preorder, postorder, level-order), balanced BSTs (AVL trees — rotations, balance factor; Red-Black trees — properties, recoloring/rotation), B-trees and B+ trees (database indexing, filesystem), heaps (min-heap, max-heap, heapify, heap sort), tries (prefix trees — autocomplete, spell checking, IP routing tables), segment trees, Fenwick trees (BIT). Hash structures: hash tables (hash functions, collision resolution — chaining, open addressing/linear probing/quadratic probing/double hashing, load factor, rehashing), bloom filters (probabilistic membership — false positives, no false negatives, applications in networking/caching), cuckoo hashing. Advanced: disjoint set / union-find (path compression, union by rank), skip lists, LRU cache implementation. For each structure: when to use it, Big O for operations, real-world applications, implementation in Python and C. Interactive visualizations: animated insert/delete/search operations, complexity comparison dashboard. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: caching chapter (LRU, eviction policies).

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Sorting and searching algorithms
sprints.notes: Sorting and searching — the classics. Comparison sorts: Bubble Sort O(n^2), Selection Sort O(n^2), Insertion Sort O(n^2) — when small/nearly sorted, Merge Sort O(n log n) — stable/divide-and-conquer, Quick Sort O(n log n) average — partition schemes (Lomuto, Hoare), pivot selection (random, median-of-three), Heap Sort O(n log n) — in-place, Shell Sort, Tim Sort (Python/Java default — hybrid merge+insertion). Non-comparison sorts: Counting Sort O(n+k), Radix Sort O(d*(n+k)), Bucket Sort O(n+k). Lower bound proof: comparison sort Omega(n log n) via decision tree model. Searching: linear search O(n), binary search O(log n) — iterative and recursive, interpolation search, exponential search, ternary search. Advanced: external sorting (for data that doesn't fit in memory), parallel sorting algorithms, sorting networks (Batcher's odd-even, bitonic sort). Stability matters: why stable sorts are important for multi-key sorting. For each algorithm: step-by-step trace, complexity analysis (best/worst/average), when to use, implementation in code. Interactive: sorting algorithm visualizer with speed controls, side-by-side race, sorting sound (auditory learning). 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: sorting chapter — the cost of ordering, when to stop sorting and start satisficing.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Greedy algorithms and dynamic programming
sprints.notes: Two foundational algorithm design paradigms. Greedy algorithms: greedy choice property, optimal substructure, proof of correctness (exchange argument, greedy stays ahead). Classic problems: activity selection (interval scheduling), Huffman coding, fractional knapsack, Dijkstra's (greedy on shortest path), Kruskal's/Prim's (greedy on MST), job scheduling with deadlines, coin change (when greedy works vs when it doesn't). When greedy fails: 0/1 knapsack, TSP, graph coloring — transition to DP. Dynamic programming: overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, memoization (top-down) vs tabulation (bottom-up), state definition, recurrence formulation. Classic DP problems: Fibonacci (the gateway), 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence (LCS), longest increasing subsequence (LIS), edit distance (Levenshtein — spell checkers, DNA alignment), coin change (minimum coins), matrix chain multiplication, rod cutting, subset sum, partition equal subset. Advanced DP: DP on trees, DP on graphs (shortest paths as DP), bitmask DP (TSP exact solution via Held-Karp O(2^n * n^2)), DP optimization (Knuth's, divide-and-conquer optimization). Security applications: DP in string matching (intrusion detection signatures), optimal resource allocation in incident response. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: optimal stopping (the 37% rule / secretary problem), explore vs exploit tradeoff.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Divide and conquer, backtracking, and recursion
sprints.notes: Algorithm design paradigms continued. Recursion mastery: recursive thinking, base cases, recursive leap of faith, call stack visualization, tail recursion, converting recursion to iteration, recursive vs iterative tradeoffs. Divide and conquer: split → solve → combine, Master theorem for analysis. Classic D&C: merge sort, quick sort, binary search, Strassen's matrix multiplication O(n^2.807), closest pair of points O(n log n), Karatsuba multiplication, median of medians (O(n) selection). Backtracking: state-space tree, pruning, constraint satisfaction. Classic problems: N-Queens, Sudoku solver, subset generation, permutation generation, graph coloring, Hamiltonian path, maze solving, word search. Branch and bound: backtracking + bounding function for optimization, 0/1 knapsack via B&B, TSP via B&B (tighter than brute force). Randomized algorithms: Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo, randomized quicksort, randomized primality testing (Miller-Rabin), skip lists, reservoir sampling, random walks. Interactive: recursion call tree visualizer, N-Queens step-through, backtracking maze solver animation. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: when to explore (backtrack) vs exploit (commit to a path).

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — String algorithms and pattern matching
sprints.notes: String algorithms — critical for security applications. Pattern matching: naive O(n*m), Rabin-Karp (rolling hash), KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt — failure function), Boyer-Moore (bad character + good suffix rules), Aho-Corasick (multi-pattern matching — used in IDS/IPS signature engines like Snort/Suricata). String data structures: suffix arrays, suffix trees (Ukkonen's algorithm), trie-based structures. Advanced: Z-algorithm, longest palindromic substring (Manacher's), regular expression engines (NFA vs DFA construction, Thompson's construction, backtracking regex engines and ReDoS — Regular Expression Denial of Service), approximate string matching (edit distance, fuzzy matching, phonetic algorithms — Soundex, Metaphone). Compression: run-length encoding, Huffman coding (revisited from greedy), LZ77/LZ78, LZW, Burrows-Wheeler Transform (BWT — used in bzip2), dictionary-based compression. Security applications: signature-based intrusion detection (Aho-Corasick in Snort), fuzzy hashing (ssdeep — context-triggered piecewise hashing for malware similarity), ReDoS vulnerability detection and prevention, data loss prevention (DLP) pattern engines. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: information theory and compression — communicating efficiently.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Applied algorithms: Algorithms to Live By modules
sprints.notes: Course track inspired by 'Algorithms to Live By' by Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths — mapping each chapter to CS concepts with hands-on applications. Modules: (1) Optimal Stopping — secretary problem, 37% rule, when to stop searching (apartment hunting, hiring, dating), explore/exploit tradeoff. (2) Explore vs Exploit — multi-armed bandit problem, epsilon-greedy, UCB1, Thompson sampling, A/B testing. (3) Sorting — cost of ordering, when NOT to sort, bucket sort for life, search vs sort tradeoffs. (4) Caching — memory hierarchy, LRU eviction, forgetting as feature not bug, cache replacement policies in OS and web. (5) Scheduling — priority queues, shortest job first, weighted completion time, context switching cost, interrupt coalescing. (6) Bayes' Rule — prior/posterior/likelihood, updating beliefs with evidence, Bayesian spam filtering, medical diagnosis. (7) Overfitting — bias-variance tradeoff, cross-validation, regularization, Occam's razor, when simple models beat complex ones. (8) Relaxation — constraint relaxation, Lagrangian relaxation, approximation algorithms, solving hard problems by solving easier ones. (9) Randomness — when randomization beats optimization, simulated annealing, Monte Carlo methods, random sampling. (10) Networking — TCP congestion control as algorithm, exponential backoff, game theory in protocol design. (11) Game Theory — Nash equilibrium, mechanism design, auction theory, price of anarchy. Each module: real-world story → CS theory → interactive simulation → coding exercise → reflection.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Computational geometry and spatial algorithms
sprints.notes: Computational geometry — algorithms for spatial problems. Fundamentals: point representation, line intersection, cross product for orientation, collinearity. Convex hull: Graham scan O(n log n), Jarvis march O(nh), gift wrapping, divide-and-conquer hull. Closest pair of points: divide-and-conquer O(n log n). Line sweep algorithms: segment intersection (Bentley-Ottmann), closest pair sweep, Voronoi diagrams, Fortune's algorithm. Spatial data structures: k-d trees (nearest neighbor search, range queries), R-trees (spatial indexing for databases), quadtrees/octrees. Range searching: 1D range trees, 2D range trees, fractional cascading. Applications: GIS (geographic information systems), collision detection (games/simulations), motion planning (robotics), geographic routing, geofencing (security — is this device inside the allowed zone?), spatial anomaly detection (unusual login locations). Interactive: convex hull visualizer, k-d tree nearest neighbor animation, Voronoi diagram generator. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: space-partitioning for efficient search.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Algorithm challenges and competition prep
sprints.notes: Competitive programming and algorithm challenge platform. Challenge tiers: Bronze (basic DS + brute force), Silver (sorting + binary search + greedy + simple DP), Gold (graphs + advanced DP + segment trees), Platinum (advanced graph theory + computational geometry + string algorithms + math). Problem sets organized by technique: implement each algorithm from the course on progressively harder problems. Weekly challenges: new problem released each week with editorial solution after deadline. Contest mode: timed problem sets simulating competitive programming contests (Codeforces, LeetCode contest, USACO style). Leaderboard: points by problem difficulty, streak tracking, speed bonuses. Interview prep track: top 100 problems organized by pattern (sliding window, two pointers, BFS/DFS, binary search, DP patterns — knapsack, LCS, intervals), with company tags (FAANG-style questions). Integration with Prime's existing challenge infrastructure (hive engine). Security-themed problems: cryptographic algorithm implementation, network routing optimization, anomaly detection in log data, brute-force complexity estimation for password cracking. 'Algorithms to Live By' bonus round: real-world optimization puzzles from the book.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Design AI/ML hub page and curriculum map
sprints.notes: Design 'The Cortex' — the AI & Machine Learning hub within House of Code. This is a combined AI + ML curriculum that teaches both the theory and hands-on implementation, with a strong cybersecurity application lens throughout. Hub page features: curriculum map showing 4 tracks — (1) AI Foundations & History, (2) Classical Machine Learning, (3) Deep Learning & Neural Networks, (4) AI for Cybersecurity. Difficulty progression: Novice (concepts, no-code tools) → Practitioner (Python + scikit-learn) → Engineer (TensorFlow/PyTorch) → Researcher (custom architectures, papers). Prerequisites: Python fundamentals (cross-reference PL-2), basic statistics/probability (cross-reference CS-2). Hero section with 'AI Timeline' interactive showing key milestones (Turing, perceptron, backprop, ImageNet, AlphaGo, GPT, diffusion models). Quick-start path for students who just want to apply ML to security vs full deep-dive. Register in content-registry.js under code house with 'ai', 'machine-learning', 'deep-learning' topics. Cross-house links to eye (detection), dark-arts (adversarial), shield (defensive AI), script (automation).

sprints.title: The Cortex — AI foundations, history, and ethical frameworks
sprints.notes: AI foundations and context. History: Turing Test (1950), Dartmouth Conference (1956), expert systems era (1970s-80s), AI winters, statistical ML renaissance (1990s-2000s), deep learning revolution (2012 ImageNet — AlexNet), transformer architecture (2017 'Attention Is All You Need'), GPT/BERT/LLM era, generative AI explosion (2022+). Core concepts: what IS intelligence (narrow vs general vs super AI), symbolic AI vs connectionist AI, knowledge representation, search algorithms (BFS, DFS, A*, minimax, alpha-beta pruning), constraint satisfaction, planning. AI categories: supervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement learning, generative vs discriminative models, parametric vs non-parametric. Ethics and governance: bias in AI (training data bias, algorithmic bias, representation bias), fairness metrics, explainability (XAI — LIME, SHAP), AI regulation (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF), responsible AI development, deepfake ethics, autonomous weapons debate, job displacement concerns. AI in cybersecurity landscape: where AI is used today (EDR, SIEM, email security, fraud detection, threat intelligence), hype vs reality, AI washing in security products. Interactive: AI timeline explorer, Turing Test simulation, bias detection exercise.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Mathematics for machine learning
sprints.notes: Essential math for understanding ML — not just using APIs, but knowing what's under the hood. Linear algebra: vectors, matrices, matrix operations (multiplication, transpose, inverse), dot product, eigenvalues/eigenvectors (PCA foundation), singular value decomposition (SVD), vector spaces, linear transformations. Calculus: derivatives (chain rule — critical for backpropagation), partial derivatives, gradients, gradient descent (batch, stochastic, mini-batch), learning rate, local vs global minima, saddle points, convexity. Probability and statistics: Bayes' theorem (revisited for ML context), probability distributions (Gaussian/normal, Bernoulli, multinomial, Poisson), maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), maximum a posteriori (MAP), expectation, variance, covariance, correlation, Central Limit Theorem, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals. Information theory: entropy, cross-entropy (loss function), KL divergence, mutual information. Optimization: convex optimization, Lagrange multipliers, constrained optimization, Newton's method, Adam optimizer intuition. Each topic taught with ML motivation first ('why do I need eigenvalues? → PCA dimensionality reduction'). Interactive: gradient descent visualizer (2D and 3D), matrix multiplication animator, probability distribution playground. Cross-references CS-2 (discrete math) for foundational overlap.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Classical machine learning: supervised learning
sprints.notes: Classical supervised learning algorithms. Regression: linear regression (closed-form solution, gradient descent, regularization — L1 Lasso, L2 Ridge, Elastic Net), polynomial regression, logistic regression (binary classification, sigmoid function, decision boundary, multi-class via one-vs-rest/softmax). Decision trees: ID3, C4.5, CART, information gain, Gini impurity, pruning (pre/post), feature importance. Ensemble methods: bagging (Random Forest — how decorrelated trees improve performance), boosting (AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), stacking. Support Vector Machines: maximum margin classifier, kernel trick (linear, polynomial, RBF, sigmoid), soft margin (C parameter), SVM for text classification. k-Nearest Neighbors: distance metrics (Euclidean, Manhattan, Minkowski, cosine), k selection, curse of dimensionality. Naive Bayes: Gaussian, Multinomial, Bernoulli — spam filtering as classic application. Model evaluation: train/test split, cross-validation (k-fold, stratified, leave-one-out), metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, confusion matrix, PR curve), overfitting vs underfitting, bias-variance tradeoff. Feature engineering: scaling (StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler), encoding (one-hot, label, target), feature selection (chi-squared, mutual information, recursive elimination). Tools: scikit-learn throughout. Security applications: malware classification, phishing URL detection, spam filtering, network traffic classification.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Classical machine learning: unsupervised learning
sprints.notes: Unsupervised learning for pattern discovery. Clustering: k-Means (initialization — k-means++, elbow method, silhouette score), hierarchical clustering (agglomerative — single/complete/average linkage, dendrograms), DBSCAN (density-based, epsilon, minPts, handling noise), Gaussian Mixture Models (EM algorithm, soft clustering), Mean Shift, spectral clustering. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (principal component analysis — eigendecomposition, explained variance, scree plot), t-SNE (visualization of high-dimensional data, perplexity parameter), UMAP (faster than t-SNE, preserves global structure), autoencoders (neural network-based reduction). Anomaly detection: statistical methods (z-score, IQR), Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, Local Outlier Factor (LOF), Elliptic Envelope, autoencoder-based anomaly detection (reconstruction error threshold). Association rules: Apriori algorithm, FP-Growth, support/confidence/lift — market basket analysis. Topic modeling: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF). Security applications: network anomaly detection (unusual traffic patterns, port scan detection, DGA domain clustering), user behavior analytics (UEBA — insider threat detection), log clustering for SIEM, malware family clustering, threat intelligence grouping. Interactive: k-Means step-through visualizer, PCA/t-SNE explorer, anomaly detection playground with synthetic data. Cross-references eye house for monitoring/detection applications.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Deep learning fundamentals and neural networks
sprints.notes: Neural networks from perceptron to modern architectures. Foundations: biological inspiration (neuron model), perceptron (single-layer, linear separability, XOR problem), multi-layer perceptron (MLP), activation functions (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, Leaky ReLU, GELU, Swish — why ReLU solved vanishing gradients). Training: forward propagation, loss functions (MSE, cross-entropy, hinge), backpropagation (chain rule applied, computational graph), gradient descent variants (SGD, momentum, RMSprop, Adam, AdamW), learning rate scheduling (step decay, cosine annealing, warmup), batch normalization, dropout, weight initialization (Xavier, He). Architecture design: fully connected layers, hidden layer sizing, depth vs width tradeoffs, skip connections (ResNet insight), universal approximation theorem. Practical deep learning: data preprocessing (normalization, augmentation), training pipeline (DataLoader, epochs, batching), overfitting mitigation (early stopping, regularization, data augmentation), hyperparameter tuning (grid search, random search, Bayesian optimization — Optuna), transfer learning (fine-tuning pretrained models). Frameworks: PyTorch (primary — tensors, autograd, nn.Module, training loop), TensorFlow/Keras (secondary — Sequential/Functional API, tf.data), comparison and when to use each. Hardware: GPU training (CUDA basics), TPU overview, cloud ML platforms (AWS SageMaker, GCP Vertex AI, Azure ML). Interactive: neural network playground (TensorFlow Playground style but built in Prime), backpropagation step-through visualizer, loss landscape explorer.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Convolutional Neural Networks and computer vision
sprints.notes: CNNs and computer vision. CNN architecture: convolution operation (filters/kernels, stride, padding, feature maps), pooling (max, average, global average), receptive field, parameter sharing. Classic architectures: LeNet (handwriting), AlexNet (ImageNet breakthrough), VGG (depth matters), GoogLeNet/Inception (width + depth), ResNet (skip connections — 152 layers), DenseNet, EfficientNet (compound scaling), MobileNet (lightweight for mobile). Tasks: image classification, object detection (R-CNN family, YOLO — You Only Look Once, SSD), semantic segmentation (U-Net, DeepLab), instance segmentation (Mask R-CNN), image generation (GANs, diffusion models). Transfer learning for vision: ImageNet pretrained models, fine-tuning strategies (freeze layers, discriminative learning rates), domain adaptation. Data augmentation: geometric transforms (flip, rotate, crop, scale), color augmentation, mixup, cutout, AutoAugment. Tools: torchvision, OpenCV, Pillow, albumentations. Security applications: CAPTCHA solving/breaking, deepfake detection (face manipulation artifacts), malware visualization (binary-to-image classification — converting executables to grayscale images), phishing page visual similarity detection, OCR for document analysis in forensics, surveillance system analysis. Interactive: CNN filter visualization (what does each layer learn?), real-time object detection demo, style transfer playground.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Recurrent Neural Networks and sequence modeling
sprints.notes: Sequence modeling — from RNNs to attention. RNN fundamentals: sequential data, hidden state, unrolling through time, vanishing/exploding gradients. LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory): cell state, gates (forget, input, output), why LSTM solves vanishing gradients. GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit): simplified LSTM, reset/update gates, GRU vs LSTM tradeoffs. Bidirectional RNNs: forward + backward context. Sequence-to-sequence: encoder-decoder architecture, teacher forcing, beam search decoding. Attention mechanism: Bahdanau attention (additive), Luong attention (multiplicative), self-attention, the breakthrough insight — 'Attention Is All You Need'. Transformers: multi-head self-attention, positional encoding, encoder-decoder structure, layer normalization, feedforward layers, why transformers replaced RNNs (parallelization, long-range dependencies). Applications: text classification, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, machine translation, time series forecasting, speech recognition basics. Security applications: log sequence analysis (detecting anomalous command sequences), network traffic time-series anomaly detection, DGA detection (character-level LSTM), malicious PowerShell command detection, predictive threat modeling. Interactive: RNN unrolling animation, attention heatmap visualizer, sequence generation demo (character-level text generation).

sprints.title: The Cortex — Natural Language Processing and LLMs

Transformer-based NLP: BERT (bidirectional, masked language model, fine-tuning for downstream tasks), GPT family (autoregressive, next-token prediction, scaling laws), T5 (text-to-text), RoBERTa, DistilBERT, XLNet. Large Language Models: architecture deep-dive (decoder-only, billions of parameters), pretraining (next-token prediction on internet-scale data), instruction tuning, RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback), Constitutional AI, DPO. Using LLMs: API usage (Claude API, OpenAI API), prompt engineering (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, system prompts), RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation — embedding, vector databases, chunking), fine-tuning (LoRA, QLoRA, full fine-tuning), agents and tool use. LLM evaluation: benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K), hallucination detection, perplexity. Security applications: phishing email detection (NLP classification), threat intelligence report parsing (NER for IoCs), security log summarization, automated vulnerability description analysis, malware report generation. Security OF LLMs: prompt injection (direct, indirect), jailbreaking, data poisoning, training data extraction, model inversion, membership inference. Cross-references dark-arts for offensive AI techniques.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Reinforcement learning
sprints.notes: Reinforcement learning — agents that learn from interaction. Foundations: agent, environment, state, action, reward, policy, value function, Markov Decision Process (MDP), Bellman equation, discount factor (gamma), exploration vs exploitation (epsilon-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling — connects to CS-10 Algorithms to Live By). Classical RL: Monte Carlo methods, Temporal Difference learning (TD(0), TD(lambda)), Q-learning (off-policy, tabular), SARSA (on-policy). Deep RL: Deep Q-Network (DQN — experience replay, target network, Atari breakthrough), Double DQN, Dueling DQN, Prioritized Experience Replay. Policy gradient methods: REINFORCE, Actor-Critic (A2C, A3C), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO — current workhorse), Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO). Advanced: multi-agent RL (MARL — cooperation, competition), model-based RL (World Models, MuZero), offline RL, reward shaping, sim-to-real transfer, RLHF for LLMs (connecting back to ML-9). Environments: OpenAI Gymnasium (CartPole, LunarLander, Atari), custom environments, PettingZoo (multi-agent). Security applications: adaptive penetration testing agents (automated attack path discovery), dynamic firewall rule optimization, adaptive honeypot behavior, intrusion response automation, adversarial RL for testing security policies, autonomous cyber defense agents. Interactive: GridWorld RL visualizer, Q-table heatmap, policy gradient training demo. Connection to Colosseum game mechanics — RL agent that could play Hexworth Arena card game.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Generative AI (GANs, diffusion models, and beyond)

Variational Autoencoders: encoder-decoder, latent space, KL divergence, reparameterization trick, VAE vs GAN tradeoffs, beta-VAE. Diffusion models: forward process (adding noise), reverse process (denoising), U-Net backbone, noise schedules, classifier-free guidance, DDPM, DDIM. Text-to-image: DALL-E, Stable Diffusion (architecture, latent diffusion, CLIP text encoder), Midjourney, controllable generation (ControlNet, IP-Adapter). Audio generation: text-to-speech (neural TTS), voice cloning, music generation. Video generation: Sora-like architectures (temporal transformers). Security implications: deepfake generation and detection (face swap, lip sync, full body), synthetic voice attacks (vishing with cloned voices), AI-generated phishing content, data augmentation for training security models (generating synthetic malware samples), copyright and IP concerns. Deepfake detection: visual artifacts, temporal inconsistencies, frequency analysis, detection models (FaceForensics++, Microsoft Video Authenticator). Cross-references dark-arts for offensive applications.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Adversarial machine learning and AI security

Data poisoning: backdoor attacks (BadNets, Trojan attacks), clean-label attacks, data poisoning for model degradation, label flipping. Model attacks: model extraction (stealing model parameters via API queries), membership inference (was this data point in training set?), model inversion (reconstructing training data), training data extraction from LLMs. Defenses: adversarial training (augmenting with adversarial examples), certified defenses (randomized smoothing, interval bound propagation), input preprocessing (feature squeezing, JPEG compression), model robustness evaluation (AutoAttack benchmark), differential privacy for training, federated learning security. ML supply chain: model serialization attacks (pickle deserialization in PyTorch — arbitrary code execution), Hugging Face model hub security, poisoned pretrained models, dependency attacks in ML pipelines. MITRE ATLAS: Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems — tactics, techniques, and case studies. Red teaming AI: systematic evaluation methodology, jailbreak taxonomies, automated red teaming. Labs: craft adversarial examples against image classifier, backdoor attack demonstration, model extraction via API queries, LLM jailbreak exercise. Cross-references dark-arts (offensive) and shield (defensive).

sprints.title: The Cortex — ML for cybersecurity: detection and defense
sprints.notes: Practical ML applications for cybersecurity defense — the blue team AI toolkit. Network security: network intrusion detection with ML (NSL-KDD, CICIDS datasets), flow-based classification, encrypted traffic analysis (without decryption — metadata, timing, size features), DGA domain detection (Random Forest, LSTM), DNS tunneling detection. Malware analysis: static analysis features (PE headers, imported functions, file entropy, string analysis), dynamic analysis features (API call sequences, system call graphs, network behavior), malware family classification, zero-day malware detection via anomaly detection, EMBER dataset. Email security: phishing detection (URL features, email header analysis, NLP on body text, visual similarity of phishing pages), BEC (Business Email Compromise) detection. User behavior analytics: insider threat detection (baseline behavior modeling, anomaly scoring), account compromise detection (impossible travel, unusual access patterns, credential abuse patterns). SOC automation: alert triage ML (priority scoring, false positive reduction), automated incident classification, SOAR integration. Threat intelligence: IoC enrichment with ML, threat actor attribution, dark web monitoring with NLP. Practical pipeline: data collection → feature engineering → model selection → training → evaluation → deployment → monitoring → retraining. MLOps for security: model drift detection, continuous retraining, A/B testing models, explainability for SOC analysts (why did the model alert?). Labs: build a phishing URL detector, train malware classifier on EMBER, anomaly detection on network flow data. Cross-references eye and shield houses.

sprints.title: The Cortex — MLOps, deployment, and production ML

CI/CD for ML: automated testing (data validation, model performance tests, A/B testing), pipeline orchestration (Kubeflow, Airflow, Prefect), feature stores (Feast), monitoring (data drift, concept drift, model degradation). Responsible deployment: model cards, bias auditing before deployment, canary deployments, rollback strategies, incident response for ML systems. Security: model serving attack surface, API authentication, rate limiting, input validation, adversarial input detection in production. Cross-references cloud house for infrastructure.
